An angel of glory announces Babylon's fall
Come out of her, my people; repay her double; her boast and sudden judgment
The kings' lament
The merchants' lament and the cargo list
The sailors' lament
Call for heaven and the saints to rejoice
The millstone sign and the silencing of the city

Revelation 18 is composed almost entirely of echoes of the prophets' oracles against Babylon and Tyre: Isaiah 13-14, 21 and 47; Jeremiah 50-51; and Ezekiel 26-28, Tyre's fall and the laments of kings, merchants and seamen. The cargo list (18:12-13) adapts Ezekiel 27:12-24, Tyre's trade list, and the millstone sign adapts Jeremiah 51:63-64, where Seraiah throws the scroll of Babylon's doom, tied to a stone, into the Euphrates. The silencing of music, mills, lamps and weddings repeats Jeremiah 25:10 (and 7:34; 16:9), words first spoken against Jerusalem and Judah. The structure is a funeral dirge (Hebrew qinah) in prophetic form, with the triple "Woe, woe" and the refrain "in one hour". Taunt-songs over fallen cities were a prophetic genre (Isaiah 14:4-21; Ezekiel 27).

Richard Bauckham's study "The Economic Critique of Rome in Revelation 18" (in The Climax of Prophecy) showed how closely the cargo list matches Rome's luxury imports: silk from China, citron wood from North Africa, ivory, cinnamon and spices via the Red Sea and India trade, Tyrian purple, marble and enormous imports of grain and slaves. Roman moralists such as Pliny the Elder complained of the drain of wealth to the East for luxuries (Natural History 6.101; 12.84) and of the craze for citron-wood tables (13.91-102). The lamenters are those who profited from the empire's economy: client kings, traders and shipowners, while the slave trade, "bodies and souls of human beings", stands at the end of the list as an indictment. Those who read Babylon as Jerusalem point instead to the wealth of the Herodian temple and its trade in sacrificial goods, priestly fabrics and incense, and to Jesus' words that the blood of the prophets would be required of Jerusalem. Futurists see a literal future commercial capital. The chapter's call to "come out of her" made it a text for Christian separation from compromised economic and religious systems throughout church history.
Another angel with great authority; the earth illuminated by his glory
Ezekiel 43:2 describes the glory of the God of Israel returning to the temple so that the earth shone with his glory. Angels reflecting God's glory appear in Daniel 10:6 and Luke 2:9.
The angel comes directly from God's presence, so the announcement carries divine authority. The glory that fills the earth contrasts with the darkness that will settle on Babylon (18:23).
Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!

Isaiah 21:9: "Fallen, fallen is Babylon, and all the images of her gods are shattered." Jeremiah 51:8 says Babylon has suddenly fallen. The cry first appears in Revelation 14:8. The prophetic past tense ("has fallen") treats a future event as certain.
Historical Babylon was taken by Cyrus in 539 BC and later declined into ruins; by John's time it was largely deserted.
A proclamation of certain judgment, using the "prophetic perfect". It announces in advance what the rest of the chapter describes.
The fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 (Gentry, Chilton), or, for preterists who identify Babylon with Rome, the judgments on Rome beginning with the crisis of AD 68-69.
The final overthrow of papal Rome, in some readings literally by fire (Elliott, Barnes).
The future destruction of the end-time city (a rebuilt Babylon or revived Rome) at the end of the tribulation (Walvoord, Thomas).
The certain doom of the world system, anticipated in every fallen empire and completed at the end of history.
A lair for demons, a haunt for every unclean spirit, bird and beast

Prophetic oracles describe ruined Babylon and Edom as inhabited by desert creatures, owls, jackals, goat-demons (se'irim) and the night creature Lilith (Isaiah 13:19-22; 34:11-15; Jeremiah 50:39; 51:37). Baruch 4:35 threatens Babylon with demons. Unclean birds are those forbidden in Leviticus 11:13-19.
Ruined cities overgrown and home to wild animals were a familiar sight in the ancient world; Babylon itself had become such a place.
Total desolation. The city that hosted luxury now hosts only unclean spirits: the opposite of the New Jerusalem, into which nothing unclean enters (21:27).
All the nations have drunk the wine of the passion of her immorality
Jeremiah 51:7 and 25:15-16: Babylon's cup made the nations mad. "Passion" (Greek thymos) can mean both passion and wrath, a wordplay: her intoxicating wine becomes God's wrath (14:8, 10).
The nations were intoxicated by what Babylon offered: power, wealth and idolatry. The wordplay hints that her seduction carries its own punishment.
The merchants of the earth grew rich from the extravagance of her luxury

Ezekiel 27-28 portrays Tyre as a merchant city whose trade led to pride and violence (Ezekiel 28:5, 16). Isaiah 23:8 calls Tyre's merchants princes. Ezekiel 27:33 says Tyre enriched the kings of the earth.

Merchants (emporoi) were long-distance wholesale traders. Rome was the greatest market of the ancient world, and trading guilds in cities such as Thyatira and Laodicea were tied to civic and imperial cults, which made participation a problem for Christians (Revelation 2:20).
Babylon's guilt includes an economic system that enriches traders through luxury. Bauckham argues that Revelation's critique is economic as well as religious and political.
The merchants who traded with Jerusalem and its temple, whose wealth Josephus describes (Chilton).
Global commerce centred on the end-time commercial capital.
A permanent warning about economic systems that serve luxury and exploit people.
Come out of her, My people

The prophets commanded the exiles to leave Babylon: Jeremiah 50:8; 51:6, 45 ("Go out of her, my people"); Isaiah 48:20; 52:11 (quoted in 2 Corinthians 6:17). Lot was told to flee Sodom (Genesis 19:12-22). Jesus told disciples in Judea to flee to the mountains when they saw Jerusalem surrounded (Luke 21:20-21).
Christians in the cities of Asia faced pressure to join trade-guild banquets, civic festivals and imperial-cult celebrations to keep their livelihood.

A call to separate from Babylon's sins so as not to share her plagues. Many interpreters understand it as moral and spiritual separation (refusing compromise) rather than geographic flight, though the latter is possible.
Christians fled Jerusalem before the siege; Eusebius reports that the Jerusalem church, warned by an oracle, moved to Pella (Ecclesiastical History 3.5.3).
A call to leave the Roman church, cited by the Reformers and later Protestants as a mandate for separation.
A literal call to believers in the end-time city to leave before its destruction.
A permanent call to refuse complicity with the world's idolatry and exploitation while living within it.
Her sins are piled up to heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities
Jeremiah 51:9: Babylon's judgment reaches to heaven. The builders of Babel wanted a tower reaching to heaven (Genesis 11:4); Ezra 9:6 speaks of guilt mounting to the heavens.
The image may echo the tower of Babel: her sins form a tower to heaven, and God, who seemed to forget, now remembers.
Pay her back double; mix her a double portion in her own cup

Jeremiah 16:18 and 17:18 speak of double repayment for sin; Jeremiah 50:15, 29 calls for Babylon to be repaid as she has done. Isaiah 40:2 says Jerusalem has received double for her sins. Exodus 22:4, 7, 9 requires a thief to repay double.

The point is full and fitting retribution. Some scholars (for example Meredith Kline) argue the Greek diplosate means "repay the equivalent" (a matching duplicate) rather than twice as much, which fits the principle "as she has done".
I sit as queen; I am not a widow and will never see grief

Isaiah 47:7-9 is the source: Babylon says she will be mistress forever and will never be a widow or lose children, but both will come in one day. By contrast, Lamentations 1:1 mourns Jerusalem as "like a widow". Tyre's pride is condemned in Ezekiel 28:2.
Rome was personified as the goddess Roma, often enthroned on coins, and celebrated as Roma Aeterna, the eternal city.
Self-glorification and the illusion of permanent security. Her proud self-confidence is exactly what will be overturned.
Jerusalem's confidence in the temple and her covenant status (Jeremiah 7:4; Matthew 3:9), refusing to see herself as a widow while she rejected her husband (Chilton).
Rome's ideology of eternal rule, Roma Aeterna (Bauckham, Koester).
The arrogance of the end-time city at the height of its power.
Her plagues will come in one day: death, grief, famine; consumed by fire

Isaiah 47:9 ("both will come in a moment, in one day"). Babylon fell to the Persians in a single night (Daniel 5:30). Fire was the fate of Sodom (Genesis 19:24) and, in the law, of a prostitute priest's daughter (Leviticus 21:9); compare 17:16.
Sieges brought death, mourning and famine together; Josephus describes the horrors of famine in besieged Jerusalem (Jewish War 5.424-438; 6.193-213).
Sudden, total destruction, in contrast to her sense of permanence. "Mighty is the Lord God who judges her" shows that no city is too strong for God.
Pestilence, mourning, famine and fire describe the siege of Jerusalem and its burning in AD 70 (Chilton, Gentry).
Some historicists expected a literal burning of Rome as the final end of the papacy (Elliott).
A literal sudden destruction of the end-time city, perhaps in a single day.
The kings of the earth weep and wail, standing at a distance: Woe, woe, the great city

Ezekiel 26:15-18 and 27:35 describe the princes and kings of the coastlands trembling and lamenting over Tyre. The lament form (qinah) appears in Lamentations and Ezekiel 27. The double "woe" (Greek ouai ouai) is a funeral cry.
Client kings depended on Rome for their thrones and wealth; the end of Rome would be the end of their own position.
The kings mourn not for the city but for what they have lost; they stand at a distance because they fear sharing her fate. Their lament is self-interested.
In a single hour your judgment has come
Isaiah 47:9, 11 (suddenly, in one day); Daniel 5:30. The ten kings rule "one hour" with the beast (17:12).
The refrain repeated by each group stresses the shocking speed of the fall. It echoes the "one hour" of the beast's allies: their brief hour of power is matched by the city's sudden hour of judgment.
The cargo: gold, silver, precious stones and pearls, fine linen, purple, silk and scarlet

Ezekiel 27:12-24 lists Tyre's trade with the nations by region and product; Revelation's list of 28 or 29 items (a multiple of seven, by some counts) adapts it. Many items were also materials of the tabernacle and temple (Exodus 25:3-7; 35:5-9).

Bauckham shows that nearly every item was a prized import to Rome: gold and silver for display, gems and pearls (Pliny calls pearls the most costly of all things, Natural History 9.106), fine linen from Egypt, purple dye from Tyre, silk from China (worth its weight in gold), scarlet from kermes. Pliny estimated that India, China and Arabia drained the empire of 100 million sesterces a year (Natural History 12.84).

The list displays the luxury that fed one city's appetite at the cost of the provinces and the poor. It moves from precious materials to food and finally to human beings, exposing the moral cost of the system.

Chilton and others note how many of the goods were used in the temple and its sacrifices (gold, purple, scarlet, fine linen, incense, spices, flour, oil, wine, cattle and sheep), suggesting Jerusalem's temple economy; critics answer that silk, ivory, citron wood, marble and the slave trade fit Rome far better (Bauckham), while preterists reply that the list is modelled on Ezekiel 27's lament over Tyre and so need not be an inventory of the city's own imports.
The wealth and trade of the papal church, including the sale of offices, relics and indulgences (Barnes).
The worldwide trade of a literal end-time commercial capital.
A portrait of consumer luxury in every civilisation that worships wealth.
All kinds of citron wood, articles of ivory, precious wood, bronze, iron and marble
Ivory and fine woods adorned Solomon's palace and throne (1 Kings 10:18-22); Amos condemned the rich of Samaria for "houses of ivory" (Amos 3:15; 6:4). Ezekiel 27:15 lists ivory traded by Tyre.

Citron wood (thyine wood, from the North African thuja tree) was the most fashionable timber in Rome; tables made from its grained roots sold for the price of an estate (Pliny, Natural History 13.91-102). Ivory came from Africa and India in great quantities for furniture and statues; coloured marble was quarried across the empire, and Augustus boasted that he found Rome a city of brick and left it of marble (Suetonius, Augustus 28).
The fittings of elite Roman houses and public buildings. These items are hard to connect with Jerusalem and are among the strongest clues for a Roman setting.
Cinnamon, spice, incense, myrrh and frankincense

Cinnamon, myrrh and frankincense were ingredients of the holy anointing oil and incense of the tabernacle (Exodus 30:23-38). The magi brought frankincense and myrrh to Jesus (Matthew 2:11). Proverbs 7:17 has the adulteress perfume her bed with myrrh and cinnamon.

Spices came by caravan from Arabia and by sea from India and Sri Lanka; the Greek amomon was an Indian aromatic used in perfumes and funeral rites. Incense burned at every pagan altar and in the imperial cult.
The perfumes of luxury, worship and seduction. For some readers, their link to the temple suggests Jerusalem; for others, their role in pagan cult and Roman banquets suggests Rome.
Incense and spices for the Jerusalem temple, a major element of its economy (Chilton).
Imports for Roman perfumes, banquets, funerals and pagan temples (Bauckham).
Wine, olive oil, fine flour and wheat; cattle, sheep, horses and chariots

Fine flour, oil and wine were offerings in the temple (Leviticus 2:1-7; Numbers 15:4-10); cattle and sheep were sacrificial animals. Solomon imported horses and chariots (1 Kings 10:28-29), which Deuteronomy 17:16 forbade kings to multiply. Compare the third seal's prices of wheat, oil and wine (Revelation 6:6).

Rome imported vast quantities of grain from Egypt and North Africa for its free grain dole; fine flour (similis) was a luxury for the wealthy. The Greek word for chariot here (rhede) denotes a four-wheeled carriage of the rich.
Even staples flowed to the capital, and luxury carriages marked the elite. Bauckham notes that Rome's grain supply sometimes left provinces short.
Slaves and souls of men

Ezekiel 27:13 says Javan, Tubal and Meshech traded "the souls of men" (human beings) with Tyre. Joel 3:3-6 condemns Tyre and Sidon for selling Judeans as slaves. The law condemned kidnapping and selling a person (Exodus 21:16; Deuteronomy 24:7; 1 Timothy 1:10).

The Greek is literally "bodies, and souls of human beings". "Bodies" (somata) was the trade term for slaves in markets and sale documents. Rome's economy depended on millions of slaves, many from conquest; after the Jewish War Josephus says 97,000 captives were taken (Jewish War 6.420).

The list ends with human beings, treated as merchandise. The addition "and souls of human beings" may be John's protest: slaves are not mere bodies but persons. It is the climax of the economic critique.
Some preterists see it as the trade in people that accompanied Jerusalem's fall and its own exploitation of the poor; others accept that the slave trade points to Rome.
A lasting indictment of every economy that treats human beings as commodities, including modern trafficking.
The fruit of your soul's desire has departed; your luxury and splendour have vanished
Compare the rich fool of Luke 12:16-21 and James 5:1-5 (the rich whose riches have rotted). Ezekiel 27:27 lists Tyre's wealth sinking into the sea.
An aside addressed directly to the city: what she craved is gone forever. The repeated "never again" (Greek ou me) begins here and continues to 18:23.
The merchants weep and mourn: clothed in fine linen and purple and scarlet
Ezekiel 27:31-36 records the merchants of the nations hissing and wailing over Tyre. The description of the city in 18:16 repeats the harlot's clothing in 17:4.
Merchants and their guilds were among the main beneficiaries of Roman peace and markets.
The merchants grieve over lost profits: they repeat the city's finery as if mourning a lost customer. The city and the harlot are clearly one.
Every shipmaster, passenger and sailor stood at a distance; they threw dust on their heads

Ezekiel 27:28-34: Tyre's pilots and sailors stand on the shore, throw dust on their heads, roll in ashes and cry "Who was ever destroyed like Tyre?" Throwing dust is a sign of mourning (Joshua 7:6; Job 2:12; Lamentations 2:10).

Rome depended on shipping, especially the grain fleets from Alexandria and the port of Ostia (and Puteoli). Shipowners were a powerful commercial class; Claudius gave them incentives to keep grain flowing (Suetonius, Claudius 18-19).

Maritime trade wept over the loss of its greatest market. Their cry "What city was ever like this great city?" echoes Ezekiel 27:32 and parodies the praise of God ("Who is like the beast?" in 13:4; "Who is like you, O LORD?" in Exodus 15:11).
Gentry and Chilton argue Jerusalem's commerce and pilgrim trade reached across the Mediterranean; critics answer that a seaborne trade centre fits Rome better.
Global shipping tied to the future capital.
Rejoice over her, O heaven, O saints and apostles and prophets

Jeremiah 51:48: the heavens and the earth will shout for joy over Babylon. Deuteronomy 32:43 calls the heavens to rejoice when God avenges his servants' blood. The legal language ("God has judged your judgment against her") suggests a court verdict in favour of the saints.
The saints rejoice not out of revenge but because God has vindicated them in a lawsuit. The mention of apostles places the persecution in the apostolic era for many interpreters.
The apostles and prophets killed by Jerusalem's leaders (Stephen, James son of Zebedee, James the Just) are vindicated in AD 70.
Peter and Paul, by tradition martyred in Rome under Nero, are among those vindicated (Bauckham, Koester).
The redeemed in heaven rejoice at the final fall of the end-time system.
A mighty angel cast a stone like a great millstone into the sea

Jeremiah 51:63-64: Seraiah ties a stone to the scroll of Babylon's doom and throws it into the Euphrates, saying Babylon will sink and rise no more. Exodus 15:5 says Pharaoh's army sank like a stone. Jesus said it would be better for one who causes little ones to stumble to have a millstone hung around the neck and be thrown into the sea (Matthew 18:6); and he spoke of a mountain being cast into the sea (Matthew 21:21).
A "great millstone" (mylos onikos) was the large stone turned by a donkey in commercial mills.
A prophetic sign-act: sudden, violent and irreversible destruction. Some preterists connect "this mountain" cast into the sea (Matthew 21:21, said near the temple mount) with Jerusalem.
Jerusalem thrown down in AD 70, never to be the centre of God's covenant worship again; some link it to Jesus' word about "this mountain" being cast into the sea (Chilton).
The final, total destruction of the end-time city.
The certain and permanent end of the godless world order.
No more harpists, flute players, trumpeters, craftsmen or the sound of a millstone

Jeremiah 25:10 (against Judah and Jerusalem) and 7:34; 16:9 speak of God silencing the sounds of joy, of bride and bridegroom, of millstones and the light of the lamp. Ezekiel 26:13 silences Tyre's songs and harps. Isaiah 24:8 ends the joy of tambourines and lyres.
Music accompanied banquets, festivals, weddings and funerals in Roman cities; trade guilds of craftsmen were central to urban life and civic religion.
The ordinary sounds of a living city fall silent: culture, work and daily bread. The repeated "never again" is a funeral knell. In contrast, heaven is filled with music (19:1-8).
Jeremiah 25:10 was spoken against Jerusalem; preterists see the same judgment repeated on the city in AD 70.
No light of a lamp; no voice of bride and bridegroom
Jeremiah 7:34; 16:9; 25:10; 33:11 (the voice of bride and bridegroom will return to restored Jerusalem). Lamps lit wedding processions (Matthew 25:1-13).

Home life and future generations end. The silence of the human wedding in Babylon prepares for the joyous wedding of the Lamb and his Bride (19:7-9) and for the city that needs no lamp because God is its light (21:23; 22:5).
Your merchants were the great ones of the earth; all nations were deceived by your sorcery

Isaiah 23:8 calls Tyre's merchants princes; Isaiah 47:9, 12 condemns Babylon's many sorceries and spells; Nahum 3:4 calls Nineveh "mistress of sorceries" who sold nations. Sorcery (pharmakeia) is listed among the sins of the unrepentant (Revelation 9:21; 21:8; 22:15).

Magic, astrology and drugs (pharmaka) were widespread in the Greco-Roman world; Ephesus was famous for magical books (Acts 19:19). "Great ones" (megistanes) were the magnates and courtiers of the empire.
Two charges: arrogance of the merchant class, and deceptive enchantment of the nations. Babylon's "sorcery" is the spell of wealth and power that blinded the world.
In her was found the blood of prophets and saints, and of all slain on the earth

Jeremiah 51:49: Babylon must fall for the slain of Israel, as the slain of all the earth fell because of Babylon. Jesus said that on Jerusalem would come all the righteous blood shed on earth, from Abel to Zechariah (Matthew 23:35-37), and that a prophet cannot perish outside Jerusalem (Luke 13:33-34).
Rome's wars and executions, including Nero's killing of Christians in AD 64, made it the great shedder of blood in the Mediterranean world.
The final verdict: Babylon is guilty not only of the blood of God's servants but of all violent death on earth. The scope is universal.

Gentry and Chilton see this as the decisive echo of Matthew 23:35 and Luke 13:33: the city guilty of the blood of the prophets is Jerusalem. Critics reply that the phrase "all who were slain on the earth" fits an imperial power better, and that Jeremiah 51:49 is the closer source; preterists answer that Jesus himself laid on Jerusalem "all the righteous blood shed on earth" (Matthew 23:35).
Papal Rome, accused of shedding the blood of martyrs over many centuries.
Every violent world power is guilty of the blood shed by the system it represents.
Rome, and every persecuting empire that follows its pattern (Bauckham, Beale).

Gentry, Chilton and others read the chapter as a dirge over first-century Jerusalem. "Come out of her" matches the flight of Christians to Pella; plagues, famine and fire match the siege of AD 70; the cargo list includes the materials and sacrificial goods of the temple economy; the silencing of bride and bridegroom repeats Jeremiah 25:10, spoken against Jerusalem; and the blood of the prophets is the charge Jesus laid on Jerusalem (Matthew 23:35). Preterists who identify Babylon with Rome read the chapter as a prophecy of Rome's judgment, beginning with the upheavals of AD 68-69.

The fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 was the decisive judgment that ended the old covenant world and cleared the way for the wedding of the Lamb in 19:7-9 (Preston, King). Critics observe that this leaves no future consummation of the kind confessed in the historic creeds; proponents reply that Scripture's time indicators bind the fulfilment to that generation.

Babylon is papal Rome, whose final destruction (in some accounts by literal fire) is still future or in progress; the call to "come out of her" was the Reformation's summons to leave Rome; the cargo list reflects the wealth and trade of the medieval church (Elliott, Barnes; earlier the Reformers and Puritans).

The chapter describes the literal destruction of an end-time commercial and political capital at the close of the tribulation. Dyer, Woods and Thomas expect a rebuilt Babylon on the Euphrates, since Isaiah 13 and Jeremiah 50-51 were not, in their view, fully fulfilled; Walvoord distinguishes the religious Babylon of chapter 17 (destroyed by the beast) from the commercial Babylon of chapter 18 (destroyed by God).

Babylon is the world as economic and cultural seductress in every age. The laments of the kings, merchants and sailors show how dependent societies become on wealth and luxury, and the call to come out of her is a permanent summons to Christians to refuse complicity (Hendriksen, Milligan).

Bauckham's influential reading sees chapter 18 as a prophetic critique of Rome's economy, built from the oracles against Babylon and Tyre, which also stands as a pattern for every exploitative world power until the final judgment. Beale, Koester and Osborne broadly agree.
Which items in the cargo list point most clearly to Rome, and which could fit Jerusalem's temple economy? How much weight should the list carry in identifying Babylon?
The kings, merchants and sailors mourn from a distance. What does their lament reveal about what they loved?
How should Christians today hear the command "Come out of her, my people" (18:4)? Is it a call to physical separation, moral distance or both?
Why does the list end with "bodies and souls of human beings"? What does that say about God's judgment on economic systems?
How does the silence of Babylon (18:22-23) prepare for the wedding of the Lamb and the New Jerusalem?
Hallelujah, the Marriage Supper and the Rider on the White Horse
Babylon's fall and the final victory (17:1-19:21)

Heaven answers Babylon's fall with the only 'Hallelujah' choruses in the New Testament, praising God's just judgment of the great prostitute and announcing that the marriage of the Lamb has come and his bride is clothed in fine linen. John is told to write a beatitude for those invited to the Lamb's marriage supper, and is rebuked for falling at the angel's feet. Heaven then opens on a rider on a white horse, Faithful and True, the Word of God, who wears many diadems and a robe dipped in blood and strikes the nations with the sword from his mouth. A grim counter-banquet, 'the great supper of God', follows as the beast and the false prophet are captured and thrown alive into the lake of fire and their armies fall by the rider's sword. Whether this is the Second Coming, a first-century judgment-coming, or a symbolic portrait of Christ's conquest through the gospel is one of the hinge questions of the book, because what follows in chapter 20 depends on it.
Heaven's Hallelujahs over the judgment of the prostitute
The marriage of the Lamb has come; the bride clothed in fine linen
Beatitude of the marriage supper; John forbidden to worship the angel
Heaven opened: the rider on the white horse, King of kings and Lord of lords
The angel in the sun summons the birds to the great supper of God
The beast and false prophet captured and thrown into the lake of fire; their armies slain

Chapter 19 stitches together two Jewish image-worlds. The first is the liturgy of Israel: the Hebrew word 'hallelujah' ('praise Yah') belongs to the Psalter, where it first appears at the close of Psalm 104 over the removal of sinners from the earth and frames the Hallel Psalms (113-118) sung at Passover, Tabernacles and other feasts. Tobit 13:18 had already pictured the streets of a rebuilt, jewelled Jerusalem crying 'Hallelujah'. The second is the prophetic picture of Israel's God as bridegroom (Hosea 2, Isaiah 54 and 62, Ezekiel 16) and as divine warrior returning from Edom with garments stained red (Isaiah 63), striking the wicked with the rod of his mouth (Isaiah 11:4) and feeding birds on the corpses of Gog's army (Ezekiel 39:17-20). Second Temple writings such as Psalms of Solomon 17, 4 Ezra 13 and the Qumran War Scroll had developed the warrior-messiah who destroys the nations by his word; the Wisdom of Solomon (18:15-16) even pictures God's all-powerful Word leaping from heaven as a stern warrior with a sharp sword. Revelation reworks these traditions around a crucified Lamb whose only weapon proceeds from his mouth.

For readers in Roman Asia the scene also mirrors and parodies imperial ceremony. Emperors were greeted with rhythmic acclamations and hailed as saviour and lord; Domitian reportedly liked to be addressed as 'our lord and god' (Suetonius, Domitian 13). A Roman triumph featured a victorious general in a chariot drawn by white horses, followed by his army and his captives, ending in the execution of enemy leaders. Royal titles like 'king of kings' were claimed by Parthian and earlier Persian monarchs beyond the Euphrates. John's vision answers all of this: the true 'Lord God Almighty' reigns, the true triumph is celebrated in heaven, the true King of kings rides out, and the empire's beast and its religious propagandist end up as the captives. The date of Revelation (before AD 70 or c. AD 95) is disputed and shapes whether interpreters hear Nero's Rome, Jerusalem, Domitian's Rome, or a future world power behind the fallen prostitute.
Hallelujah!

Transliterated Hebrew hallelu-yah, 'praise Yah(weh)'. It belongs to the Psalter: its first occurrence closes Psalm 104 after a prayer that sinners vanish from the earth, and it frames Psalms 105-106, 111-113, 115-117 and 146-150. Psalms 113-118 (the 'Egyptian Hallel') were sung at Passover, Pentecost and Tabernacles (Mishnah Pesahim 10 describes the Passover use; written later but reflecting temple practice). Tobit 13:18 pictures the streets of a restored Jerusalem singing 'Hallelujah' — a close Second Temple parallel to Revelation's sequence of hallelujahs leading into the jewelled New Jerusalem.

Greco-Roman cities greeted emperors and governors with rhythmic shouted acclamations (Latin acclamationes) celebrating their victories and benefactions. John's heavenly crowd acclaims God, not Caesar, for the true victory.

These are the only occurrences of 'hallelujah' in the New Testament. The fourfold cry (19:1, 3, 4, 6) is heaven's response to the prayers of the martyrs (6:10) and to the call to rejoice over Babylon (18:20). Judgment is praised because it is 'true and just' and vindicates God's servants, and the climax turns from judgment to the reign of God and the wedding of the Lamb. The worship is Passover-shaped: a new exodus celebrated with Israel's festival praise.
